a: The record of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah
p: The Hebrew title can mean 'words' or 'deeds, history.' It marks what follows as Nehemiah's own account.
b: Divre means "words," but in titles it often means "affairs" or "history," as in "the scroll of the records of the kings of Israel" (1 Kings 14:19), where "records" is the same word. The same phrase opens Jeremiah and Amos, where it introduces a prophet's words, and Ecclesiastes. Here it heads a first-person account: from 1:1 to 7:5 Nehemiah speaks as "I." Scholars call this the Nehemiah memoir. It continues in parts of 12:27–43 and 13:4–31. In the Hebrew Bible Ezra and Nehemiah were one book, so this title marks a new section inside it, not a new book. Hacaliah is otherwise unknown; the name may mean "wait for the LORD."

a: the month of Kislev in the twentieth year
p: Kislev 446 BC and Nisan 445 BC on the usual reckoning, both in one 'twentieth year.'
b: Kislev is the ninth month, about November–December; Nisan (2:1) is the first, about March–April. The year is not named here, but 2:1 and 5:14 show it is the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, almost always taken as Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC). That makes Kislev come before Nisan in the same "twentieth year." Explanations: Nehemiah counted the king's years from his accession in late 465, not from Nisan as Babylon did; or he dated by a fall-to-fall calendar like the later Jewish one; or 1:1 once read "nineteenth." Most scholars accept one of the first two, which put this Kislev in late 446 BC and the audience of 2:1 in Nisan 445 BC. Harold Hoehner counted the regnal years from Tishri in a way that gives Kislev 445 and Nisan 444 BC. On the date and on Artaxerxes I or II, see the chapter page.

a: the fortress at Susa
p: Susa was one of the Persian kings' capitals, used in winter. Its fortified palace stood on a raised mound.
b: Susa (Hebrew Shushan), in what is now southwest Iran, was the old capital of Elam. Darius I built a great palace there, and the Persian kings spent the winter months in it. Birah means a fortress or fortified palace on a high mound; Esther uses the same phrase, "Susa the fortress" (Esther 1:2), and Daniel has his vision there (Daniel 8:2). French excavations since 1884 uncovered Darius's audience hall (the apadana) and a foundation text recording the peoples who brought materials for it. A Jewish official at Susa was not unusual: Babylonian business records show Judeans in royal service.

a: One of my brothers, Hanani
p: Hanani is called Nehemiah's brother again in 7:2. The word can mean a kinsman, but here probably a real brother.
b: "Brother" in Hebrew can mean a kinsman or a fellow Jew (as in 5:1), but 7:2 calls Hanani "my brother" in a way that suggests a real brother, and Nehemiah later gives him charge over Jerusalem. An Aramaic letter from Elephantine in Egypt (the "Passover Papyrus," 419 BC) mentions a Hananiah who sends instructions to the Jews there about the Feast of Unleavened Bread; some scholars think he may be the same man, and that he held an office for the Jews under Persian rule. That identification is possible but not proven.

a: the Jews who had escaped, the ones left from the captivity
p: Two words of the prophets for the people saved through judgment: those who escaped and those who were left.
b: Peletah ("those who escaped") and nish'aru ("were left," the root of "remnant") are prophetic words for the people who survive God's judgment (Isaiah 10:20; Ezra 9:8; Ezra 9:15). Nehemiah asks about the community in Judah, mostly families who had come back from Babylon over the past ninety years (Ezra 1–2) and also those who had never been taken. The word "Jews" (yehudim), first meaning people of Judah, becomes common in Ezra–Nehemiah and Esther as the name of the people as a whole.

a: Jerusalem's wall is breached, and fire has burned its gates
p: Was this the ruin of 586 BC, or a fresh disaster? Many think Hanani reports the wall stopped in Ezra 4.
b: Babylon burned Jerusalem and tore down its walls in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9–10), 140 years earlier. Nehemiah's grief would be strange if this were old news. So many scholars link the report with Ezra 4:7–23: under Artaxerxes, officials in Samaria complained that the Jews were rebuilding the walls, the king ordered the work stopped, and they forced it to stop "with force and might" (Ezra 4:23), perhaps destroying what had been built. Others think Nehemiah was simply learning, perhaps for the first time from eyewitnesses, how bad things still were. Either way the walls were a sign of shame (cherpah) before the nations.

a: fasting and praying before the God of the heavens
p: A title used mostly in Persian-period books, where Persian officials also used it. Nehemiah uses it often.
b: "The God of the heavens" appears in Cyrus's decree (Ezra 1:2) and in letters between Jews and Persian officials (Ezra 5:11–12; Ezra 7:12). The Elephantine letters use the Aramaic form, "the God of heaven," in a petition to the Persian governor (about 407 BC). It was a title both Jews and Persians could understand: the God who rules all. Nehemiah uses it in his prayers (1:4–5; 2:4) and before his opponents (2:20). His fasting and mourning follow a pattern of Persian-period piety (Ezra 9:3–5; Daniel 9:3; Esther 4:3).
r: Ezra 1:2; Ezra 5:11–12; Ezra 7:12; Daniel 2:18–19; Jonah 1:9; 2:4; 2:20; Daniel 9:3; Esther 4:3

a: Please, LORD
p: Where the Hebrew has God's personal name, YHWH, this translation prints 'the LORD' in capitals.
b: The four Hebrew letters YHWH are God's own name, revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14–15). By the time of the Greek translation, Jews read it aloud as Adonai, "Lord," out of reverence, and most English Bibles follow by printing "the LORD" in small capitals. Where the Hebrew has Adonai itself, as in 1:11 and 4:14, this translation has "Lord." The name is pronounced "Yahweh" by most scholars. Anna, "please," opens the prayer with an urgent plea, as in Moses' prayer (Exodus 32:31).

a: who keeps his covenant and his loyal love with those who love him and keep his commands
p: Nehemiah begins with Moses' words: God 'keeps his covenant and his loyal love ... with those who love him.'
b: The opening of the prayer repeats Deuteronomy 7:9: "He keeps his covenant and his loyal love for a thousand generations with those who love him and keep his commands." "Great and fearsome God" comes from Deuteronomy 7:21 and 10:17. The same opening is used in Daniel's prayer (Daniel 9:4) and in a prayer of the Levites (9:32). Such prayers of confession, built from phrases of Deuteronomy and Kings, became a standard form in the Persian period (Ezra 9; Nehemiah 9; Daniel 9). Hesed, "loyal love," is God's faithful kindness within the covenant.

a: let your ear listen closely and your eyes be open
p: Nehemiah borrows Solomon's words at the dedication of the Temple: 'Keep your eyes open ... and listen.'
b: Solomon prayed, "Night and day keep your eyes open toward this house" and "Keep your eyes open to the pleas of your servant and the pleas of your people Israel" (1 Kings 8:29; 1 Kings 8:52). Solomon had also asked that if Israel sinned and went into exile and then "take it to heart and turn back," God would hear and forgive (1 Kings 8:46–50). Nehemiah, an exile praying far from the Temple, does what Solomon described. His "day and night" also echoes Solomon's "night and day" (1 Kings 8:29).

a: for the Israelites, your servants
p: The Hebrew eved means servant or slave. Here it is an honor: Israel belongs to God and serves him.
b: Eved covers a range: a slave, a hired servant, a royal official ("the king's servant") and a worshiper of God. The word occurs eight times in this prayer, for Nehemiah (1:6; 1:11), for Moses and for Israel, the language of Moses ("Moses your servant," 1:7–8). In 2:10 the same word is used of Tobiah, perhaps as an official's title or perhaps as an insult; see there. The Plain uses "servant" or "slave" by context (5:5 has slaves).

a: I and my father's family have sinned
p: Nehemiah confesses sins he did not personally commit, joining himself to Israel's whole history.
b: Nehemiah was born in exile and served a foreign king faithfully, yet he does not say "they sinned" but "we." Leviticus 26:40 had said that in exile the people "will confess their guilt and their fathers' guilt." Ezra (Ezra 9:6–7), Daniel (Daniel 9:5–11) and the Levites (9:2; 9:33–35) pray the same way. In Jewish prayer the confession (viddui) of the Day of Atonement is likewise said in the plural. Christian readers have often seen in such prayers a model of intercession, the leader standing with the people before God.

a: the commands, the rules and the rulings
p: The three nouns are Deuteronomy's terms for the whole law: commands, rules and rulings.
b: Mitzvot, chuqqim and mishpatim are the vocabulary of Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 5:31; Deuteronomy 6:1; Deuteronomy 7:11). This translation renders them the same way across the Bible: "commands," "rules" and "rulings." The verb before them, chabal, means to act destructively; doubled in Hebrew it makes "we have done terrible wrong."

a: 'You will act unfaithfully, and I will scatter you among the peoples.
p: The 'word to Moses' is not a single verse. It sums up Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 4, 28 and 30.
b: No one passage says exactly this. Nehemiah gathers Moses' warnings and promises: "The LORD will scatter you among the peoples" (Deuteronomy 4:27; compare Deuteronomy 28:64; Leviticus 26:33), and "from there you will search for the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 4:29). Ma'al, "act unfaithfully," is the priestly word for breaking faith with God (Leviticus 26:40). Chronicles uses it for the sins that led to the exile (1 Chronicles 9:1; 2 Chronicles 36:14). Nehemiah reminds God of his own word: if the warning came true, so can the promise.
r: Leviticus 26:33; Leviticus 26:40–45; Deuteronomy 4:27–31; Deuteronomy 28:64; 1 Chronicles 9:1; 2 Chronicles 36:14

a: Even if your scattered people are at the farthest edge of the sky, I will gather them from there
p: Nehemiah quotes Moses' promise of return almost word for word, then joins it to 'the place I have chosen.'
b: Deuteronomy 30:2–4 says, "You and your children will turn back to the LORD your God ... Even if you have been driven to the farthest edge of the sky, the LORD your God will gather you from there." Nehemiah adds Deuteronomy's phrase for Jerusalem's Temple, "choose a place to make his name live there" (Deuteronomy 12:11). For Nehemiah, the place is Jerusalem, and the promise is already partly kept: exiles have come back. The phrase "edge of the sky" pictures the horizon, the farthest place on earth.

a: You ransomed them by your great strength and your mighty hand
p: 'Ransomed' and 'mighty hand' are Deuteronomy's words for the exodus from Egypt.
b: Moses prayed, "they are your people, your inheritance, whom you brought out by your great power and your outstretched arm" (Deuteronomy 9:29), and "you ransomed" them (Deuteronomy 9:26; Deuteronomy 15:15). Nehemiah uses the same appeal: these exiles are the same people God once freed from Egypt. Ezra–Nehemiah often tells the return from Babylon as a second exodus (Ezra 1:4–6; 9:9–21).

a: this man
p: Nehemiah calls the most powerful king on earth simply 'this man.' Before God the king is only a man.
b: The prayer ends with an abrupt "this man," the king Nehemiah will face. Many readers hear a deliberate contrast: before the God of the heavens even the king of Persia is just a man, whose heart God can turn (Proverbs 21:1). Others take it simply as a pointer: the prayer was spoken over months (1:1; 2:1) and its last line looks to the coming audience. Both readings fit. "Compassion" (rachamim) is the word Solomon used when he asked that captors would show the exiles pity (1 Kings 8:50).

a: the king's cupbearer
p: The cupbearer tasted and served the king's wine. It was a post of high trust and often of real influence.
b: Greek writers describe the Persian cupbearer as one of the king's closest servants. Herodotus says the cupbearer of Cambyses had great honor, and the apocryphal book of Tobit says Ahiqar was "chief cupbearer" and finance minister to the Assyrian king (Tobit 1:22). Pharaoh's cupbearer appears in Genesis 40. The cupbearer guarded the king against poison, saw him daily, and could speak to him at ease. The Greek of Nehemiah in some manuscripts reads eunouchos, "eunuch," for oinochoos, "cupbearer"; Rahlfs prints "cupbearer" (checked). Edwin Yamauchi argues that Nehemiah need not have been a eunuch; others point to 6:11 and the queen's presence in 2:6.

a: It was the month of Nisan
p: Many Christians count Daniel's seventy weeks from this month; Jewish and critical readers count otherwise.
b: Daniel 9:25 dates seventy "sevens" from "a word to bring back and build Jerusalem" (freshly translated). Many Christians take that word to be Artaxerxes' permission here: Julius Africanus (preserved by Eusebius), Robert Anderson, who counted from Nisan 445 BC, and Harold Hoehner, who counted from Nisan 444 BC. Others count from Ezra 7, as Isaac Newton did, or from Cyrus, and Jerome already listed rival counts. Most critical scholars read Daniel 9 as written about 165 BC, with no reference to Nehemiah. Rashi counts the 490 years from the First Temple's fall to the Second's, on the rabbinic chronology of Seder Olam. See the chapter page.

a: in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes
p: Most scholars date this to spring 445 BC, under Artaxerxes I Longimanus.
b: Three Persian kings were named Artaxerxes. Nehemiah's is almost certainly Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC). An Elephantine letter of 407 BC names "the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria" and the high priest Johanan (12:22), which fits Nehemiah's opponent a generation earlier. The twentieth year of Artaxerxes I ran from spring 445 to spring 444 BC, so Nisan was March–April 445. Nehemiah stayed until the thirty-second year, 433 BC (5:14; 13:6). Only a few scholars put him under Artaxerxes II (404–359 BC). On this verse and Daniel's seventy weeks, see the chapter page.

a: Until then I had never looked sad before him
p: A servant who looked gloomy before the king could seem disloyal. The Hebrew may mean he had never been sad there before.
b: Persian court rules kept a cheerful face before the king; Esther 4:2 says no one could enter the king's gate in sackcloth. The Hebrew lo hayiti ra' lefanav is short and allows two readings: "I had not been sad in his presence before," which explains the king's surprise, or, with a small change, "I was not (allowed to be) sad before him." Some think Nehemiah let his grief show on purpose, choosing the moment to raise his request. Four months had passed since Kislev (1:1), perhaps waiting for the right occasion, such as a banquet.

a: This must be a troubled heart and nothing else
p: The Hebrew says 'badness of heart,' which can mean sorrow or, in a court, a hidden plot.
b: Roa' lev is literally "badness of heart." Ecclesiastes 7:3 uses the same noun for a sad face: "by sadness of face the heart is made better." But the phrase could also hint at bad intentions, and a cupbearer with a secret grievance was a danger to the king. That may be why Nehemiah "became terribly afraid." He answers by blessing the king and naming his grief openly.

a: The city that holds my ancestors' graves
p: Nehemiah does not name the city. He speaks of family graves, which any Persian would honor.
b: Nehemiah avoids the name Jerusalem before the king, perhaps because the same king had recently stopped its walls from being rebuilt as a "rebellious and evil city" (Ezra 4:12–22). Instead he appeals to the honor owed to ancestors' tombs, a value Persians shared. The tombs of the kings of Judah were in the City of David (3:16; 2 Chronicles 32:33), so the phrase may also hint that Nehemiah was of royal descent, as some scholars suggest; the text does not say.

a: So I prayed to the God of the heavens
p: Nehemiah prays silently in the moment before he answers the king. His book is full of such quick prayers.
b: Between the king's question and his answer Nehemiah prays, with no words recorded. The four months of prayer in chapter 1 come down to this moment. The memoir shows the same habit again and again: short prayers in the middle of action (4:4–5; 4:9; 5:19; 6:9; 6:14; 13:14; 13:22; 13:29; 13:31). Christian writers have often held up "arrow prayers" like this one as a model; readers also note that the book joins two kinds of prayer, the long set prayer (1:5–11) and the cry of the moment.

a: while the queen sat at his side
p: The word means a royal wife (see the variant). Her presence may mean a private meal.
b: Shegal is a queen or royal consort (Psalm 45:9; Daniel 5:2–3). Greek writers say Artaxerxes I's queen was Damaspia, and that his mother Amestris had great influence at court. Persian kings did not usually dine with their wives in public, so many think this was a private meal, where a trusted servant could speak more freely. Some suggest the queen helped Nehemiah's cause, but the text says only that she was there.

a: once I had named a time
p: He set a time, but 5:14 says he governed twelve years. Perhaps the term was extended, or the first time was longer.
b: Nehemiah gives the king a date for his return, but he stays as governor from the twentieth to the thirty-second year (5:14), then goes back to the king and later returns (13:6–7). Most think he first asked for a short leave, which became an appointment as governor. The wall took fifty-two days (6:15), but the work on the city and its people took far longer.

a: the governors of Beyond the River
p: The Persian province west of the Euphrates, with governors under it in Samaria, Ammon and elsewhere.
b: Ever hannahar, "Beyond the River," is the official name of the Persian province west of the Euphrates (Ezra 4:10–11). It was divided into smaller provinces under governors, such as Samaria, Judah, Ammon and Ashdod, whose leaders appear in 4:7. A traveler needed letters to pass through each district and draw supplies. An Aramaic letter of the Persian official Arsames, from about 410 BC, orders officials along a route to give rations to his steward Nehtihor, a close parallel to what Nehemiah asks.

a: Asaph, who keeps the king's park
p: The Hebrew word is pardes, a Persian loanword for a walled park. It gave us the word 'paradise.'
b: Pardes comes from Old Persian pairidaeza, "walled enclosure." Persian kings and governors kept such parks, planted with trees and stocked with game; Greek writers called them paradeisoi. The Greek of Genesis 2 used the same word for the garden of Eden, which is how "paradise" came to mean heaven (Luke 23:43). The word appears in the Bible only here, Ecclesiastes 2:5 and Song of Songs 4:13. Where this park was is unknown; some suggest a royal forest in Lebanon, others a royal estate near Bethlehem. Asaph, a Hebrew name, may have been a Jew.
r: Ecclesiastes 2:5; Song of Songs 4:13; Genesis 2:8; Luke 23:43; Revelation 2:7

a: the gates of the temple's fortress
p: A fortified tower guarded the Temple's north side. It was later rebuilt as the Baris and then the Antonia.
b: The Hebrew says "the fortress that belongs to the house," meaning the Temple. 7:2 names Hananiah as its commander. It probably stood on the north side of the Temple, the side with no valley to protect it, near the towers of Hananel and the Hundred (3:1). The Hasmoneans later rebuilt it as the Baris, and Herod rebuilt it again as the Antonia fortress, where Paul was held (Acts 21:34). The Greek lacks the fortress here; see the variant.

a: for my God's good hand was on me
p: The same words describe God's help to Ezra. Both books credit God, not the king, with every gift.
b: Ezra says, "Because the LORD his God's hand was on him, the king gave him whatever he requested" (Ezra 7:6), and "His God's good hand was on him" (Ezra 7:9; compare Ezra 8:18). Nehemiah repeats the phrase in 2:18. In both books, God works through Persian kings without miracles: the king grants, but the true giver is God. Proverbs 21:1 puts it in a saying: "The king's heart lies in the LORD's hand."
r: Ezra 7:6; Ezra 7:9; Ezra 7:28; Ezra 8:18; Ezra 8:22; 2:18; Proverbs 21:1

a: army commanders and horsemen
p: Ezra had been ashamed to ask the king for soldiers. Nehemiah accepts them. The text judges neither.
b: Ezra said, "I was ashamed to ask the king for a troop and horsemen to help us against an enemy on the way," because he had told the king that God protects those who seek him (Ezra 8:22). Nehemiah, a royal official going as governor, travels with an armed escort. Readers have compared the two: some praise Ezra's faith, others Nehemiah's good sense, and many note that the situations differed, since Nehemiah went with royal authority to a post that was already contested. Nehemiah himself makes no comment; he simply records the king's provision.

a: Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite
p: Sanballat governed Samaria; Tobiah was an official of Ammonite origin. Both families gave names honoring the LORD.
b: Sanballat (Babylonian Sin-uballit, "the moon god Sin has given life") was governor of Samaria; an Elephantine letter of 407 BC names "Delaiah and Shelemiah, the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria." His sons' names honor the LORD. "The Horonite" may mean he came from Beth-horon, northwest of Jerusalem, or from Horonaim in Moab. Tobiah ("the LORD is good") was later given a room in the Temple by the high priest (13:4–9). Tobiah the servant may mean "the king's servant," an official title like those on seals, or it may be Nehemiah's sneer, "Tobiah the slave." Readers debate whether these men were enemies of God's people or local rulers defending their own power; see the topic page.

a: to seek good for the Israelites
p: The phrase echoes Deuteronomy's 'seek their peace and their good.' It also carries the idea of a treaty.
b: Tovah, "good," can mean welfare, and in treaty language "good" means friendly relations. Deuteronomy 23:6 says of the Ammonites and Moabites, "Never seek their peace or their good," a law Nehemiah later reads aloud (13:1–3). Here the tables are turned: an Ammonite is upset that someone has come to seek the good of Israel. The irony may be deliberate.

a: Then I rose by night, taking a few men with me
p: Nehemiah inspects the walls in secret, so that no one, friend or enemy, can stop or spread his plan.
b: Nehemiah tells no one in Jerusalem what he intends (2:12; 2:16). Some of the city's leaders were tied to Tobiah by marriage and letters (6:17–19), so a plan spoken too soon would have reached his enemies. He rides alone, with a few men on foot, around the southern part of the city.

a: by the Valley Gate, past Serpent Spring, as far as the Dung Gate
p: He goes out on the west side, south along the Hinnom valley, then up the Kidron on the east. Only the south is traced.
b: The Valley Gate opened on the Tyropoeon or Hinnom valley on the west side of the City of David (2 Chronicles 26:9). The Dung Gate was near the southern tip, where refuse went out to the Hinnom valley; 3:13 puts it a thousand cubits (about 1,500 feet) from the Valley Gate. Serpent Spring is otherwise unknown; some identify it with En-rogel, below the city where the valleys meet. Then Nehemiah turns north up the Kidron (2:15), past the Spring Gate and the King's Pool near Siloam (2:14), and finds the slope so choked with fallen stone that his animal cannot pass. Excavations on the eastern slope have found the collapsed terraces and houses of 586 BC.

a: Serpent Spring
p: Tannin means a serpent or sea dragon. Some read 'jackal.'
b: Tannin is the word for Aaron's staff turned into a serpent (Exodus 7:9) and for the great sea creatures (Genesis 1:21); so "Dragon Spring" or "Serpent Spring." A similar word, tan, means jackal, which gives "Jackal Well." On the Greek "spring of the figs," see the variant. The name may recall a legend or a snake-shaped rock; nothing more is known.

a: the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the deputies
p: Nehemiah names the groups of the city: nobles (chorim), officials (seganim), priests and the people at large.
b: Chorim, "nobles" (literally "free men"), were the heads of leading families, and seganim, "officials," a Babylonian loanword, were local administrators. They appear together again in 4:14, 4:19, 5:7 and 7:5. The nobles were also the creditors in chapter 5 and Tobiah's correspondents in 6:17. Nehemiah's memoir often lists the groups he deals with, showing a society with an elite and a mass of farmers and laborers.

a: so we are not a laughingstock anymore
p: Cherpah means public shame, the scorn of neighbors. Nehemiah's word for Jerusalem's state since 1:3.
b: Cherpah is the shame of being mocked, as when Philistines taunted Israel (1 Samuel 17:26) or nations scorned the ruined city (Psalm 79:4; Lamentations 5:1). The broken walls were not only a military problem but a sign that the LORD's city was despised. The word links 1:3, 2:17, 4:4 and 5:9: Nehemiah builds to remove disgrace from God's name and people.

a: Geshem the Arab
p: Geshem is probably the 'Geshem king of Qedar' named on a silver bowl from Egypt. Qedar ruled the desert trade routes.
b: A silver bowl from Tell el-Maskhuta in the eastern Nile Delta, dated about 400 BC, bears the Aramaic words "Qaynu son of Geshem, king of Qedar," and an inscription from Dedan in northwest Arabia also names a Geshem. Most scholars identify him with Nehemiah's Geshem ("Gashmu" in 6:6). Qedar was an Arab kingdom that controlled the incense trade through the Negev and southern Judah under the Persians. A strong Jerusalem could threaten its trade. Nehemiah thus faced rivals north (Samaria), east (Ammon), south (Arabs) and west (Ashdod, 4:7).

a: Are you in revolt against the king?
p: The same charge had stopped the building before: 'the rebellious and evil city' (Ezra 4:12).
b: In Ezra 4:12–16, officials of Samaria had warned Artaxerxes that Jerusalem was "the rebellious and evil city" and that if its walls were finished it would stop paying tribute. Sanballat and his allies now raise the same charge, which had worked before. Nehemiah's answer (2:20) avoids the political question entirely: he appeals to God, not to the king's letters, perhaps because the opponents had no right to see them. The charge returns in Sanballat's open letter (6:6–7).

a: no share in Jerusalem, no rightful claim and no memorial there
p: Three legal and religious terms: no part in the land, no legal right, and no remembrance in the city's worship.
b: Cheleq, "share," is a portion of land or inheritance (2 Samuel 20:1). Tsedaqah here means a legal right (2 Samuel 19:28). Zikkaron, "memorial," may mean a name remembered in the Temple's worship or records (Exodus 28:12; Zechariah 6:14). Together they shut the opponents out of Jerusalem's land, law and worship. Many readers see a needed line around a fragile community; others note that Sanballat and Tobiah worshiped the LORD and had ties in Jerusalem, so the words also claim the right to decide who belongs, as in Ezra 4:3.
r: Ezra 4:3; 2 Samuel 20:1; 2 Samuel 19:28; Exodus 28:12; Zechariah 6:14; Acts 8:21

a: Eliashib the high priest
p: The high priest and his fellow priests start the work at the gate nearest the Temple. Eliashib reappears in 13:4.
b: Eliashib was the grandson of Jeshua, the high priest of the first return (12:10). By starting at the Sheep Gate, north of the Temple where sheep came in for sacrifice (John 5:2), the priests take the part closest to their own work. They "made it holy," consecrating the gate, the only section of the wall said to be consecrated in this chapter. Later Eliashib gives Tobiah a room in the Temple courts (13:4–7), and his grandson marries Sanballat's daughter (13:28). Chapter 3 never says whether he was already tied to Nehemiah's enemies; readers who know chapter 13 notice the irony.

a: Tower of the Hundred they made it holy, as far as the Tower of Hananel
p: The list runs counterclockwise around the city, from the Sheep Gate in the north back to the Sheep Gate (3:32).
b: The chapter starts at the Sheep Gate, moves west past the Fish Gate and the Jeshanah Gate, south along the western side to the Valley Gate and Dung Gate, up the eastern side past the Water Gate and the Horse Gate, and back to the Sheep Gate (3:32). The towers of the Hundred and of Hananel guarded the north, where the ground offered no valley for defense; Jeremiah 31:38 and Zechariah 14:10 name the Tower of Hananel as a landmark of the city to be rebuilt. The list names about forty sections and about ten gates.

a: The men of Jericho built beside him
p: Builders came from towns across the province: Jericho, Tekoa, Gibeon, Mizpah, Zanoah, Beth-zur, Keilah.
b: The list shows almost the whole community at work: priests, Levites, temple servants, goldsmiths, perfume makers and traders; district officials with their people; families repairing the stretch in front of their own houses; and men from towns outside Jerusalem. The towns named roughly mark out the Persian province of Judah, from Jericho in the east to Gibeon and Mizpah in the north and Beth-zur and Keilah in the south. The districts (pelekh, 3:9–18) were probably the province's administrative units. Tamara Eskenazi sees the chapter as a sign that the book's hero is the people as a whole, not one leader.

a: The sons of Hassenaah
p: Probably the same group as 'Senaah' in the list of returnees, here with the Hebrew article.
b: The list of returnees has "descendants of Senaah," 3,630 in Ezra 2:35 and 3,930 in 7:38. Hassenaah is the same name with the article "the." The Fish Gate, which they built, was on the north side, near the market where men of Tyre later sold fish (13:16; Zephaniah 1:10).

a: Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz
p: Hakkoz was one of the priestly families who could not prove their line (7:63). Meremoth served as a priest.
b: The family of Hakkoz could not find its records and was kept from the priesthood until a ruling could be made (7:63–65; Ezra 2:61–63). Yet Meremoth son of Uriah, of this family, received the Temple treasure as a priest in Ezra's day (Ezra 8:33), and here repairs two sections (3:21). The family seems to have been restored. Meshullam son of Berechiah later became Tobiah's in-law (6:18).

a: their nobles would not put their necks under the work of their masters
p: The plural may mean human overseers, Nehemiah and his officials, or God, 'their Lord.'
b: The image is of an ox refusing the yoke (Jeremiah 27:11; Jeremiah 27:12). Adonehem is plural, "their masters," which may mean the officials directing the work, including Nehemiah. But the plural form is also used of God ("Lord of lords," Deuteronomy 10:17), and some read "the work of their Lord." Tekoa lay near the southern border, close to Geshem's Arabs, which may explain its nobles' reluctance. The ordinary men of Tekoa did double duty (3:27). The Greek has transliterated the Hebrew word for "their nobles" as if it were a name (checked on die-bibel.de).

a: the Jeshanah Gate
p: The name may mean 'the gate of the old (city)' or 'the gate toward Jeshanah,' a town to the north.
b: Sha'ar hayshanah is literally "the gate of the old" (feminine). The KJV has "the old gate." Since the adjective does not agree with "gate," many think it means "the gate of the old (city)" or "the gate of Jeshanah," a town about 15 miles north (2 Chronicles 13:19), toward which the road led. It was on the northwest side, and appears again in 12:39.

a: which belonged to the seat of the governor of Beyond the River
p: Either Mizpah was under the governor of the larger province, or the wall reached his residence in Jerusalem.
b: The Hebrew lekisse, "to/of the throne (seat) of," is unclear. Many take it to mean that the men of Gibeon and Mizpah belonged to the jurisdiction of the governor of the large province Beyond the River (BSB, "under the authority of"). Others read "as far as the seat (residence) of the governor," a building in Jerusalem used when he visited. Mizpah had been the capital of Judah under Gedaliah after 586 BC (2 Kings 25:23), and excavations at Tell en-Nasbeh, probably Mizpah, show it thriving in the Babylonian and early Persian periods.
orig: לְכִסֵּא פַּחַת עֵבֶר הַנָּהָר (lekisse pachat ever hannahar)

a: They made Jerusalem whole again as far as the Broad Wall
p: The verb usually means 'leave, abandon.' Some think they left part of the old city outside the new wall.
b: Vayya'azvu normally means "they left" or "abandoned." One view: the builders left a part of the city outside, building a shorter wall. Another: there is a second Hebrew verb with the same letters meaning "repair, restore," known from Ugaritic and South Arabian, used here and perhaps in Exodus 23:5. The Broad Wall itself was found in 1970–71 by Nahman Avigad in the Jewish Quarter: a wall about 23 feet thick, built in Hezekiah's time. It lies well west of the smaller Persian-period city, which supports the idea that Nehemiah's wall did not take in the western hill.

a: the official over half the district of Jerusalem
p: The province was divided into districts, some split into halves, each under an official (sar).
b: Pelekh appears only in this chapter in this sense; a similar word in Akkadian means a district or a work duty. The chapter names the districts of Jerusalem, Beth-haccherem, Mizpah, Beth-zur and Keilah, several with two halves (3:9; 3:12; 3:16–18). Some scholars think pelekh means a labor gang owed to the state, which would fit a building project. Seal impressions stamped "Yehud" and the names of governors show how the Persian province was run.

a: he and his daughters
p: The only women named among the builders. Some suggest a family with no sons; the text says only 'his daughters.'
b: In a list of men, Shallum's daughters stand out. Some think Shallum had no sons, so his daughters inherited his duty and property, as Zelophehad's did (Numbers 27:1–11). Others take "daughters" as villages belonging to a town, as often in Hebrew ("Heshbon and its daughters," Numbers 21:25), but with a person's name that is less natural. Either way the verse shows women in the building work. Modern readers often note it.

a: a thousand cubits of the wall
p: A cubit was about 18 inches, so a thousand cubits was about 1,500 feet, nearly a third of a mile.
b: A cubit was the length from elbow to fingertip, about 18 inches (45 cm). The stretch from the Valley Gate to the Dung Gate was much longer than other sections. Perhaps this part of the wall had survived better, needing only repair, or perhaps the people of Zanoah were many. The whole Persian-period wall was probably about two miles around.

a: the Pool of Shelah by the king's garden
p: Shelah is the same name as Siloam, the pool fed by Hezekiah's tunnel, near the royal gardens at the city's south end.
b: Shelach means a channel or conduit, and the Greek form is Siloam (Isaiah 8:6, "the waters of Shiloah"; John 9:7). Hezekiah's tunnel carried water from the Gihon spring to a pool at the south end of the City of David (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30). A large stepped pool of the Second Temple period was found there in 2004. The king's garden lay below, where the Kidron and Hinnom valleys meet (2 Kings 25:4). The Greek here reads differently: "the pool of the fleeces at the king's shearing" (checked on die-bibel.de).
r: Isaiah 8:6; John 9:7; 2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30; 2 Kings 25:4; Jeremiah 39:4; 2:14

a: Nehemiah son of Azbuk
p: Not the governor. The name, 'the LORD comforts,' was common.
b: This Nehemiah, head of half the Beth-zur district in the south, is a different man. So is the Nehemiah of the returnees' list (7:7). The tombs of David were on the eastern hill, the City of David (1 Kings 2:10); no royal tomb has been found with certainty. "The pool that had been dug" may be a reservoir Hezekiah built (Isaiah 22:11), and "the Warriors' House" a barracks, perhaps of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:8).

a: worked hard to repair
p: The Hebrew word is uncertain; it is usually read 'eagerly.' See the variant.
b: Hecherah is usually taken as "he burned (with zeal)," so "eagerly" or "zealously." But no other builder is praised this way, which is why some doubt the word; see the variant for the Greek and a proposed change.

a: the temple servants who lived on the Ophel
p: The Hebrew netinim means 'those given.' They did the lowest work in the Temple and lived near it on the Ophel.
b: Netinim, "the given ones," were a class of Temple workers below the Levites (Ezra 8:20). Many of their family names are foreign (7:46–56); a tradition traces them to the Gibeonites, whom Joshua made "the ones who cut wood and carried water for the community and for the altar of the LORD" (Joshua 9:27). The Ophel was the ridge between the City of David and the Temple. The Hebrew of 3:26 says the temple servants "were living" on the Ophel but has no verb of repairing, so it may be a note on where they lived (as 11:21 says), with Pedaiah's section running to the Water Gate. The Plain supplies "worked," taking them as working with Pedaiah, as many translations do.

a: the Water Gate on the east
p: This gate faced the Gihon spring. The square inside it became the place where Ezra read the law (8:1).
b: The Water Gate was on the eastern side, above the Gihon spring, the city's main water source. In front of it was an open square where the people gathered to hear Ezra read the law (8:1; 8:3), and where booths were built for the feast (8:16). The procession at the dedication ended here (12:37). Some think the Persian-period wall ran higher up the slope than the old wall of the monarchy, so that the Water Gate was a gate of the older line no longer in use.

a: a member of the goldsmiths' guild
p: Hebrew 'son of' often means a member of a trade or group. So 'son of the goldsmith' means a goldsmith.
b: Ben-hatsorphi is literally "son of the goldsmith." As "sons of the prophets" means members of a prophetic band (2 Kings 2:3), "son of" a trade means a member of its guild. The goldsmiths (3:8; 3:32), perfume makers (3:8) and traders (3:31–32) worked in organized groups, as craftsmen did across the ancient Near East. The traders' section near the Sheep Gate fits the market traffic of the northern gates (13:16).

a: the Miphkad Gate
p: Miphkad means a counting, an appointed place or a mustering. The gate's purpose is uncertain.
b: The noun comes from paqad, "to count, appoint, inspect." It may have been the gate where troops or people were mustered, or where visitors were inspected; Ezekiel 43:21 uses the word for an appointed place outside the sanctuary where the sin offering was burned. It stood on the northeast, near the Temple. The KJV keeps the Hebrew name, as the Plain does.

a: the Sheep Gate
p: The circuit closes where it began, at the Sheep Gate. In John's Gospel a pool with five porches lay near it.
b: The list ends at the gate where it began (3:1). In the time of Jesus the Sheep Gate was near the pool of Bethesda with its five porches (John 5:2), which excavations north of the Temple mount have uncovered. The Masoretes marked 3:32 as the middle verse of the whole book of Ezra–Nehemiah.

a: Word reached Sanballat
p: In the Hebrew Bible, 4:1–6 is the end of chapter 3 (3:33–38), and 4:7–23 is 4:1–17.
b: The Hebrew Bible ends chapter 3 with the story of Sanballat's mockery and Nehemiah's prayer (Hebrew 3:33–38) and starts chapter 4 with the plot of the enemies (Hebrew 4:1). English Bibles follow the Latin Vulgate, which put the break at Sanballat's anger. This site uses the English numbers. Jewish translations such as the JPS follow the Hebrew.

a: In front of his brothers and the army of Samaria
p: Sanballat speaks before the troops of the province of Samaria, probably a garrison or militia.
b: Persian governors kept local forces. Sanballat's speech before "his brothers," his fellow officials or kinsmen, and "the army of Samaria" is a public show of contempt, meant to boost his own side and to frighten the Jews when the words reached them. The Greek gives a shorter speech: "Is this the strength of Samaria, that these Jews are building their city? Will they sacrifice or eat in their place?" (checked on die-bibel.de).

a: Will they fix it up by themselves?
p: The Hebrew may mean 'Will they leave it to themselves?', 'Will they restore it?' or 'Will God let them?'
b: Haya'azvu lahem uses the same verb as 3:8, which can mean "leave" or "restore." Readings: "Will they restore (the wall) for themselves?"; "Will they be left alone (by us) to do it?"; or "Will they leave it to their God?" (with "to God" understood). The next questions mock their hopes: will they sacrifice, as if a dedication were near, finish in a single day, or make burned limestone, which crumbles in fire, into building stone again?

a: If a fox went up on it, he would breach their wall of stones
p: Tobiah's joke: the wall is so weak a fox could topple it. Foxes and jackals prowled ruined cities.
b: Foxes (or jackals; the Hebrew shu'al covers both) haunt ruins in the Bible: "on Mount Zion, which is desolate; foxes walk about on it" (Lamentations 5:18, freshly translated; compare Ezekiel 13:4). Tobiah's taunt joins the joke to that picture of Jerusalem as a ruin. Excavated stretches thought to belong to Nehemiah's wall in the City of David are rough and narrow, a few feet thick, built quickly, though their dates are debated.
r: Lamentations 5:18; Ezekiel 13:4; Song of Songs 2:15; Judges 15:4

a: Listen, our God! We have become something to sneer at.
p: Nehemiah asks God to punish his enemies and not forgive them. Readers have struggled with this prayer.
b: The prayer belongs with the psalms that ask God to repay enemies (Psalm 79:12; Psalm 109:14; Jeremiah 18:23). Defenders note that Nehemiah does not take revenge himself but hands the case to God, and that mocking the builders was mocking God's work. Critics, ancient and modern, find it harsh; Jesus taught his followers to pray for their enemies (Matthew 5:44; Luke 23:34). Many see an honest prayer from people under real threat, kept in Scripture though not offered as a model in every way. "In a land where they are captives" asks that the mockers suffer the exile the Jews had suffered.
r: Psalm 79:12; Psalm 109:14; Psalm 123:3–4; Jeremiah 18:23; Matthew 5:44; Luke 23:34; Romans 12:19; 6:14; 13:29

a: Do not cover up their wrongdoing
p: Nearly the same words as Jeremiah's prayer against his persecutors.
b: Jeremiah prayed, "Do not cover their wrongdoing, and do not wipe out their sin from before you" (Jeremiah 18:23, freshly translated). Nehemiah borrows the prayer of a prophet persecuted for his message. "They have stirred up anger in front of the builders" may mean they provoked God by insulting the builders to their faces, or that they provoked the builders themselves; the Hebrew has no object.

a: to half its height
p: The wall was closed all the way around but only half as high as planned, enough to provoke the next plot.
b: "Linked up" means the gaps between sections had been closed, so the wall made a full circle, even if only to half its planned height. The image of 4:7, walls "healing" as new flesh grows over a wound (arukhah, as in Jeremiah 30:17), shows what alarmed the enemies.

a: the Arabs, the Ammonites and the people of Ashdod
p: Enemies on all sides: Samaria north, Ammon east, the Arabs south and Ashdod west.
b: Ashdod, the old Philistine city, was the center of a Persian province on the coast. With Samaria (Sanballat), Ammon (Tobiah) and the Arabs of Qedar (Geshem), Jerusalem was ringed on every side by neighbors hostile to its rebuilding. Some of Jerusalem's own people had married into Ashdodite families (13:23–24).

a: We prayed to our God, and because of them we kept watchmen posted
p: Prayer and a guard together. The verse became a classic text on trusting God while taking action.
b: Nehemiah does not choose between prayer and defense. Christian preachers, from the Puritans on, have used the verse to teach that faith works through means; a later proverb, "Trust God and keep your powder dry," makes the same point. The New Testament joins the two in "Keep watch and pray" (Matthew 26:41). Compare the later rabbinic rule that one does not rely on a miracle (Bavli Pesachim 64b), which the Talmud states without reference to Nehemiah.

a: The porters' strength has stumbled
p: Judah's complaint has the rhythm of a lament, perhaps a song the workers sang as they carried rubble.
b: The Hebrew has a short-line rhythm, the qinah or lament meter of Lamentations. It may be a work song turned sour. The sabbal was the porter who carried loads on his back (2 Chronicles 2:2). Kashal, "stumble," pictures them falling under the weight. The rubble of the 586 BC destruction, still lying on the eastern slope, had to be cleared before stones could be laid. The Greek reads "the strength of the enemies is broken" (checked on die-bibel.de), a very different sense.

a: ten times, "From all the places where you turn back, they are upon us."
p: The Hebrew is hard. It may be the villagers' warning, or their plea that the men come home.
b: Literally: "they said to us ten times, from all the places that you return, upon us." One reading: the Jews living near the enemies warned again and again that attacks would come from every side. Another, with a small change, has them urging their own men in Jerusalem to come home and defend their villages (see the variant). "Ten times" means many times (Genesis 31:7; Numbers 14:22).

a: Remember the Lord, the great and fearsome one
p: Nehemiah speaks like Moses and Joshua before battle: do not fear, the great God is with you.
b: "Do not tremble before them, because the LORD your God is among you, a great and fearsome God" (Deuteronomy 7:21). Moses told Israel, "The LORD will fight for you" (Exodus 14:14), and Nehemiah ends his next speech with "Our God will fight for us" (4:20). The call to fight "for your brothers, your sons and daughters, your wives and your houses" makes clear what was at stake: not a building but families.

a: half my young men worked at the job
p: His 'young men' were his personal servants or bodyguard, probably brought from Persia.
b: Ne'aray, "my young men," means his attendants, probably the governor's household and guard (5:10; 5:16; 13:19). Half worked and half stood armed. The "coats of armor" (shiryonim) were scale armor, as Goliath wore (1 Samuel 17:5). Nehemiah's orders turned a building site into a camp.

a: the other hand gripping a weapon
p: A famous picture of work and watchfulness. Jewish and Christian readers have both used it.
b: The image of builders with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other became proverbial. Christian writers used it for the believer's life of work and spiritual warfare (Ephesians 6:10–18). In modern Israel the picture has often been applied to settlers who built and stood guard at the same time. In the text it is practical: those carrying loads kept one hand free; the builders, who needed both hands, wore swords (4:18).

a: The man who blew the ram's horn was next to me
p: The shofar is a ram's horn, blown to call people to battle or worship. Here it is an alarm.
b: The shofar was blown at Jericho (Joshua 6:4), by Gideon (Judges 7:18) and on feast days (Leviticus 25:9). It could be heard far along the wall. The trumpeter stayed with Nehemiah so that the alarm would come from the one in command.

a: Each man's weapon was with him at the water
p: The Hebrew ends with two odd words: 'each his weapon, the water.' Many fix the text.
b: Literally "each his weapon the water." Readings: each took his weapon to the water, that is, even when going to drink or wash; or, with small changes, "in his right hand" or "even at night." The Greek lacks the whole clause; see the variant. The Plain keeps the Hebrew words with the most natural sense: the weapon went with him even to the water. The point is clear: no one let down his guard.

a: cried out loudly against their brothers, the Jews
p: Tsa'aqah is the cry the oppressed raise to God, the cry of Israel in Egypt and of the poor in the law.
b: Tsa'aqah is the outcry of the oppressed: Israel in Egypt (Exodus 3:7–9) and the poor who cry to God against a harsh lender: "When he cries out to me, I will hear, for I am gracious" (Exodus 22:27). Here the cry is not against foreigners but against fellow Jews. The wives cry too, since women and children bore the brunt of debt slavery (5:5). The chapter breaks into the wall story, perhaps because the work itself, with men away from their fields, made the crisis worse, or because Nehemiah gathered his acts of justice here; many think the events took place later in his twelve years.

a: Counting our sons and daughters, there are many of us
p: The Hebrew says 'we are many.' A small change gives 'we are pledging our sons and daughters.'
b: The three groups in 5:2–4 seem to rise in distress: families too large to feed, farmers mortgaging land, those borrowing to pay taxes. The Hebrew of 5:2 reads rabbim, "many." Many scholars change one letter to read orevim, "pledging," matching 5:3: "We are pledging our sons and daughters to get grain." The Plain keeps the Hebrew; see the variant.

a: in this famine
p: Drought, taxes and the wall's labor drove small farmers into debt. Debt led to the loss of land and children.
b: Haggai had described drought and failed harvests two generations earlier (Haggai 1:6–11). In an economy where most people farmed small plots, a bad year meant borrowing grain at interest, pledging the field, and finally selling children into service. Babylonian and Persian contracts show the same pattern. The prophets had condemned it: "they sell a righteous man for silver, a needy man for the price of sandals" (Amos 2:6, freshly translated).
r: Haggai 1:6–11; Amos 2:6; Amos 8:6; 2 Kings 4:1; Isaiah 5:8; Micah 2:2

a: the tribute to the king
p: Persia taxed its provinces in silver. Farmers short of coin had to borrow to pay.
b: Middah is the tribute owed to the crown (Ezra 4:13; Ezra 4:20; Ezra 7:24, where priests are exempt). Herodotus lists the satrapy Beyond the River as owing 350 talents of silver a year. Taxes in silver forced farmers to sell or borrow, and money lenders, often the local elite, profited. Some historians think Persian taxation was the main cause of the crisis; others stress local greed. Nehemiah's own reform targets the lenders, not Persia.

a: We are made of the same flesh as our brothers
p: The poor appeal to kinship: 'Our flesh is like our brothers' flesh.' The law forbids treating a brother as a slave.
b: "Flesh" means family, as when Laban says to Jacob, "You really are my bone and my flesh" (Genesis 29:14). The law of Leviticus says of a poor Israelite who sells himself, "do not make him work the work of a slave" (Leviticus 25:39), "For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. They must not be sold the way a slave is sold" (Leviticus 25:42). Exodus 21:2–11 and Deuteronomy 15:12 allowed debt service for six years, then release. The complaint is that the richer Jews are treating fellow Jews as property.
r: Genesis 29:14; Leviticus 25:39–43; Exodus 21:2–11; Deuteronomy 15:12; Jeremiah 34:8–17; Isaiah 58:7

a: Some of our daughters are slaves already
p: Girls were often the first to be handed over for debt, as servants or as wives for the creditor's household.
b: Exodus 21:7–11 regulates a daughter sold as a slave woman, who could become a wife of the master or his son. Elisha helped a widow whose creditor was coming to take her two children as slaves (2 Kings 4:1). Ancient Near Eastern contracts show daughters given in pledge before sons. The mothers' cry (5:1) is about their own children.

a: You are lending on pledge, each of you against his own brother!
p: The Hebrew massa' may mean interest charged on a loan or the pledge taken as security. Both broke the law's spirit.
b: Massa' ... nose'im comes from nasha, "lend on credit." The KJV and BSB have "usury"; NIV "interest"; Williamson and others argue it means making loans against pledges, seizing land and children when the debt was not paid. The law forbade charging interest to a poor brother: "Do not take interest or profit from him. Fear your God" (Leviticus 25:36; compare Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 23:19–20). Deuteronomy limited what a lender could take as a pledge (Deuteronomy 24:10–13). Nehemiah's appeal to "the fear of our God" (5:9) echoes Leviticus 25:36.

a: I called a great assembly
p: Nehemiah takes the matter out of private dealings into a public assembly, where shame and oath can work.
b: Nehemiah first confronts the nobles and officials directly, then calls a great assembly (qehillah). The public setting puts the lenders under the eyes of the whole people and prepares for the oath before the priests (5:12–13). The procedure recalls the covenant-making assemblies of Israel's history (2 Kings 23:1–3; Jeremiah 34:8–10).

a: We have done what we could to buy back our Jewish brothers who were sold to the nations
p: Jews in exile had been buying fellow Jews out of slavery to foreigners. Now Jews were enslaving Jews at home.
b: The law gave a kinsman the right to buy back a relative who had sold himself to a foreigner: "after he has sold himself he still has the right to be bought back. One of his brothers may redeem him" (Leviticus 25:48). Nehemiah says that he and others, probably in the eastern diaspora, had done this at their own cost. The irony is sharp: the lenders in Judah sell brothers who must then be redeemed again. In later Jewish law, the redeeming of captives (pidyon shevuyim) became one of the highest duties of charity.

a: to keep the nations, our enemies, from scorning us
p: Injustice among God's people gives their enemies a reason to mock God. Nehemiah ties ethics to witness.
b: The same enemies who mocked the walls (4:1–4) could now mock a people who enslaved their own kin. The appeal echoes the prophets: God's name is "profaned among the nations" because of Israel's conduct (Ezekiel 36:20–23). Paul uses similar logic: "Because of you, God's name is spoken against among the nations" (Romans 2:24, freshly translated).

a: I myself, my brothers and my young men are lending them silver and grain as well
p: Nehemiah admits his own household was lending too. Was he confessing, or saying his loans were fair?
b: Some readers hear a confession: Nehemiah himself had been part of the system and now gives it up first. Others think he means he lent without interest or pledges, and so can urge others to stop. The verb "let us drop" includes himself either way. Readers have often praised a leader who starts with his own house.

a: give them back their fields, vineyards, olive trees and houses
p: Returning the land is what the law's release years were meant to do. Nehemiah enacts one at once.
b: Deuteronomy commanded a release of debts every seventh year: "Every lender is to let go of the loan he made to his neighbor" (Deuteronomy 15:2). Leviticus 25 returned land to its families in the Jubilee: "he and his children with him. He will go back to his clan" (Leviticus 25:41). Nehemiah does not wait for a calendar year. Jeremiah 34:8–22 tells of an earlier release in Zedekiah's day that the owners broke; Nehemiah binds his with an oath and a curse (5:12–13). The people later pledge to keep the seventh-year release (10:31).

a: the hundredth part of the silver
p: Probably the interest: one percent a month, twelve percent a year. Some read 'the debt' with a small change.
b: Me'at is "the hundredth." Interest was often stated by the month, and one percent a month was a common rate; Babylonian rates for silver were often higher, around 20 percent a year. Some scholars change one letter to read "the debt" (see the variant), so the lenders cancel the loans themselves. "New wine and fresh oil" (tirosh and yitshar) are the standard pair of the harvest, as in Deuteronomy 7:13.

a: I also shook out the front of my robe
p: An acted curse: as the robe's fold is emptied, so God will empty the man who breaks his oath.
b: The chotsen was the fold of the robe at the chest, used as a pocket. Shaking it out pictured a man shaken out of his house and property. Prophets often acted out their words (Jeremiah 13:1–11; Ezekiel 4–5). Paul and Barnabas shook dust from their feet against a city that rejected them (Acts 13:51), and Paul shook out his clothes at Corinth (Acts 18:6). The people's "Amen" accepts the curse on themselves, as in Deuteronomy 27:15–26.

a: from King Artaxerxes' twentieth year to his thirty-second
p: 445–433 BC. The verse was written after his term ended, looking back.
b: Nehemiah was appointed governor (pechah) of the province of Judah, a post others had held before him (5:15), perhaps including Zerubbabel (Haggai 1:1) and governors known from seals and jar stamps such as Elnathan. The verse looks back over the whole term, so this part of the memoir was written after 433 BC. Whether Judah had its own governors before Nehemiah, or had been run from Samaria, is debated; seal impressions with governors' names suggest it had.

a: The earlier governors who came before me weighed the people down
p: The Talmud faults Nehemiah for speaking badly of earlier governors, among them, it says, Daniel.
b: Nehemiah contrasts his own generosity with the greed of his predecessors. The Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 93b) says the book was not called by Nehemiah's name (it was part of "Ezra") because he took credit to himself ("Remember me for good," 5:19) and because he spoke against those before him, even Daniel, whom the rabbis counted among them. Modern scholars are divided: some read the memoir as a self-serving defense (Clines, "the perils of autobiography"); others see a sincere account of a governor who used his own wealth to serve. Persian-period records show that governors did live on taxes from their provinces.

a: forty shekels of silver on top of that
p: The Hebrew 'after silver, forty shekels' is odd. It may mean 'besides' or 'at the rate of' forty shekels a day.
b: Literally "they took from them in bread and wine, after silver shekels forty." Readings: "besides forty shekels of silver" (KJV, BSB); "forty shekels of silver a day" (with a small change); or "for the price of" that much silver. The Greek has "last" or "at the end," perhaps reading a similar word (checked on die-bibel.de). A shekel weighed about 0.4 ounces (11.5 grams).

a: one ox, six of the best sheep and some birds
p: Feeding 150 men plus guests cost far more than most could afford. Nehemiah paid it himself.
b: Solomon's daily provisions were much larger (1 Kings 4:22–23), but Nehemiah's table fed about 150 officials and leading Jews plus visitors (5:17), as was expected of a governor. Persepolis tablets record daily rations for Persian officials and their households. Nehemiah says he paid for this without drawing the governor's allowance, because "the labor lay heavy on this people," the forced labor or service owed by the province.

a: My God, remember me for good
p: The first of Nehemiah's 'remember me' prayers. A plea for reward, or a request that God see what he has done?
b: The memoir has four prayers that God remember Nehemiah (5:19; 13:14; 13:22; 13:31), two of them "for good" (5:19; 13:31), which have the same Hebrew and the same English, and two that God remember his enemies (6:14; 13:29). Sigmund Mowinckel and Gerhard von Rad compared votive and memorial inscriptions, where a donor asks a god to remember his gifts; on this view the memoir was written to be laid before God. Ulrich Kellermann read it instead as the prayer of an accused man defending himself. The rabbis criticized his self-praise (Bavli Sanhedrin 93b). Many Christian and Jewish readers see an honest plea: in Hebrew, "remember" means to act on someone's behalf (Genesis 8:1; Exodus 2:24), and Nehemiah trusts God, not people, to judge his record.

a: at Kephirim, in the valley of Ono
p: Ono lay near Lod, about 25 miles northwest of Jerusalem, on the border of Samaria and Ashdod.
b: Ono was near Lod (7:37; 11:35; 1 Chronicles 8:12), on the coastal plain at the edge of Judah's settlements, in border land between provinces. A meeting there would take Nehemiah a day's journey from Jerusalem, into territory where his enemies were strong. Kephirim may be a village name, or the common word "villages" (so the Greek, checked on die-bibel.de, and NIV). Nehemiah saw the trap: "They meant to do me harm."

a: It is a big work I am doing, and I am not able to come down
p: Nehemiah refuses with dignity: his work is too great to leave. The line became a favorite sermon text.
b: The reply avoids accusing his enemies, which might give them grounds for complaint, and keeps the moral high ground. "Come down" also fits the land: Jerusalem stands high, Ono low. Christian preachers have often used the verse to urge people not to be distracted from God's calling; in Jewish homiletics, too, Nehemiah's focus is held up as a model.

a: an open letter
p: Letters were normally sealed. An open letter meant its charges could be read by anyone along the way.
b: Official letters were rolled, tied and sealed; Aramaic letters from Elephantine and the Arsames archive still carry their seals. Sanballat sends his fifth message open, so that its accusation of rebellion would spread, whether or not Nehemiah answered. It was a threat dressed as friendly advice: "Now the king is going to hear about all this" (6:7).

a: Gashmu
p: The same man as Geshem (2:19; 6:1), in an Arabian form of the name with its old ending.
b: Gashmu keeps the old Arabian (North Arabian) nominative ending -u. It is the form in the Hebrew here; 2:19 and 6:1–2 have Geshem. The inscribed bowl from Tell el-Maskhuta has the short form, "Geshem" (Gashm).

a: you have set up prophets to announce about you in Jerusalem, 'A king in Judah!'
p: Prophets had once hailed Zerubbabel as God's chosen ruler. A Jewish governor with a royal title would alarm Persia.
b: Two generations before, Haggai had called Zerubbabel God's "signet ring" (Haggai 2:23) and Zechariah spoke of a "Branch" who would rule (Zechariah 6:12–13). Prophets in Jerusalem might well have hoped for a king again, and some, like Noadiah (6:14), opposed Nehemiah. Sanballat's charge was dangerous because it was plausible; Persia put down revolts in Egypt in Artaxerxes' reign. Nehemiah's reply is a flat denial (6:8).

a: So now, make my hands strong!
t: A prayer, or 'I strengthened my hands'?
p: The Hebrew is a command, best read as a short prayer to God.
b: The enemies hope the Jews' hands will "go limp" (rafah). Nehemiah answers with the opposite verb, chazzeq, "strengthen." The Hebrew form is a command, addressed to no one; most read it as a prayer to God (some English versions add "O God"). The Greek reads it as a statement; see the variant. Compare 2:18, "They made their hands strong," the same verb.

a: He was shut away indoors
p: Why Shemaiah was 'shut in' is unclear: ritually unclean, acting out a prophecy, or pretending to be in danger.
b: Atsur means "held back, restrained." Some think Shemaiah was in a state of ritual impurity, kept from the Temple (compare Jeremiah 36:5, where Jeremiah is "restrained"). Others see a prophetic sign: shutting himself in to show the danger, so that Nehemiah would come to him. Others again think he pretended to fear for his own life. His message has the short, rhythmic form of a prophetic oracle, as the Plain's repeated last lines show.

a: inside the sanctuary
p: Only priests could enter the hekhal, the main hall of the Temple. A layman who went in would sin.
b: Hekhal is the main hall of the Temple, the Holy Place, where only priests could go (Numbers 18:7). King Uzziah was struck with a skin disease for entering it (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Nehemiah was not a priest. Hiding there would have been a sin (6:13) and would have shown him as a coward. The altar offered asylum to those who took hold of it (1 Kings 1:50; 1 Kings 2:28), but that was in the court, not the sanctuary.

a: And who like me could go into the sanctuary and stay alive?
p: Either 'to save his life,' or 'and live,' since a layman who entered would deserve death.
b: Vachay can mean "and save his life" (NIV) or "and live" (KJV). The second reading points to the law: "The outsider who comes near is to be put to death" (Numbers 18:7; compare Numbers 3:10). Some have suggested a further reason: if Nehemiah was a eunuch, as some think (see 1:11), he would have been barred even from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1). Most think the priestly rule is enough.

a: because Tobiah and Sanballat were paying him
p: Balaam was hired to curse Israel. Micah: 'its prophets divine for silver.'
b: The law warned against prophets who lead astray (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:20–22), and Moab "hired Balaam son of Beor ... to curse you" (Deuteronomy 23:4). Micah said of Jerusalem, "its prophets divine for silver" (Micah 3:11, freshly translated). Nehemiah's test is the content: God would not tell him to break his law. Shemaiah may have been one of the prophets who wanted a king (6:7), or simply a man for hire.
r: Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:20–22; Deuteronomy 23:4; Micah 3:5; Micah 3:11; Jeremiah 23:16; 13:2

a: Noadiah the prophetess
p: A woman prophet who opposed Nehemiah, one of very few women called prophets in the Hebrew Bible.
b: Noadiah ("the LORD has met") is one of the few women called a prophet in the Hebrew Bible, with Miriam (Exodus 15:20), Deborah (Judges 4:4), Huldah (2 Kings 22:14) and Isaiah's wife (Isaiah 8:3). Nothing else is known of her. On the Greek, which makes Noadiah a man, see the variant; a man named Noadiah appears in Ezra 8:33. Her opposition suggests that some of Jerusalem's prophets saw Nehemiah, the Persian king's man, as an obstacle to their own hopes (6:7).
r: Exodus 15:20; Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14; Isaiah 8:3; Ezra 8:33; Luke 2:36; 6:7

a: The wall was done in fifty-two days
p: Elul 25 is early October. Was fifty-two days possible? Josephus says two years and four months.
b: If the work began in the month Av, the wall was finished on the 25th of Elul (about October 2, 445 BC). Josephus says the wall took two years and four months (Antiquities 11.179), perhaps counting all the work on the city. Most scholars accept fifty-two days for closing the circuit, since much of the old wall's base could be reused, the city was smaller than in the monarchy, and the whole province worked at once. The memoir gives the credit to God (6:16).

a: they sank low in their own eyes
p: A rare expression for losing heart. The Greek reads 'fear fell on them greatly.'
b: Literally "they fell greatly in their eyes." The phrase is found nowhere else; it seems to mean that the enemies lost their confidence or prestige. The Greek has "fear fell greatly in their eyes" (checked on die-bibel.de). "Were afraid" (vayyir'u) could also be read, with different vowels, as "they saw," which some prefer: "all the nations around us saw it."

a: Many people in Judah had sworn loyalty to him
p: Tobiah was tied to leading families by marriage and by oath. He was an insider as well as an outsider.
b: Ba'ale shevu'ah, "lords of an oath," may mean allies bound by a sworn agreement, perhaps a business partnership or marriage covenant. Shecaniah son of Arah belonged to a family of returnees (7:10), and Meshullam son of Berechiah had worked on the wall (3:4; 3:30). Tobiah's own name and his son's, Jehohanan ("the LORD is gracious"), honor the LORD. Later the Tobiad family became powerful in Ammon and Jerusalem (2 Maccabees 3:11; Josephus, Antiquities 12.160–236).

a: Gatekeepers, singers and Levites
p: The Temple's gatekeepers guarded the city gates for a time, with the singers and Levites.
b: Gatekeepers normally guarded the Temple gates (1 Chronicles 26:1–19). Here, with singers and Levites, they seem to be set over the city gates too, at least until local watches could be organized (7:3). Some scholars think "the singers and the Levites" were added by an editor who expected them in such lists (compare 7:43–45; 12:45–47).

a: I gave charge over Jerusalem to my brother Hanani and to Hananiah
p: Hanani and Hananiah may be two men, or one with two forms of his name.
b: Hanani is a short form of Hananiah ("the LORD has been gracious"). Most read two men: Nehemiah's brother (1:2) and the fortress commander (2:8). Some read "Hanani, that is, Hananiah," one man described twice. The reason given, "a man you could trust," is singular in Hebrew, which slightly favors the reading in which the praise belongs to Hananiah.

a: until the sun grows hot
t: Open late, or shut at midday?
p: Most read: do not open until the sun is high. Some read: do not leave them open in the heat of noon.
b: "Until the sun is hot" usually means "until well after sunrise," when the city is fully awake. Others take ad as "while": "do not open the gates while the sun is hot," that is, close them at midday, when guards and townspeople rested (compare 2 Samuel 4:5, an attack in the heat of the day). On the Greek "until sunrise," see the variant. The second half of the verse, which the Plain also follows, has the guards shut the doors while they are still on duty, at evening.

a: only a few people lived inside it
p: Jerusalem had walls but few people. Chapter 11 tells how Nehemiah filled it by lot.
b: Excavations suggest that Persian-period Jerusalem was small, perhaps a few hundred to perhaps 1,500 people, mostly on the eastern ridge, with the Temple to the north. "The houses were not built yet" may mean few houses stood, or that families had not built homes inside the walls. This verse sets up the census (7:5) and the resettlement of 11:1–2, where one in ten of the people is chosen by lot to live in the city.

a: I came across the family register of those who had come up first
p: Nehemiah finds the register of the first returnees. It is nearly the same list as Ezra 2.
b: What follows (7:6–73) repeats Ezra 2:1–70 with small differences. Nehemiah presents it as an old document, "those who had come up first," found when he planned a new enrollment. Scholars debate the borrowing: Williamson argues that Ezra took the list from Nehemiah, because the list's ending (7:73) fits Nehemiah's story, where the seventh month follows naturally (8:1); others think Nehemiah took it from Ezra, or that both drew on a Temple archive. See the chapter page for the differences, and the notes on Ezra 2.

a: Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani
p: Nehemiah's list has twelve leaders, Ezra's eleven. Many think twelve was the original, one for each tribe.
b: Nehemiah adds Nahamani and has Azariah for Ezra's Seraiah, Raamiah for Reelaiah, Mispereth for Mispar and Nehum for Rehum. 1 Esdras 5:8 also has twelve. Twelve leaders for a community that saw itself as all Israel (7:73) fits the twelve offerings of Ezra 6:17 and 8:35. The Nehemiah named here is not the governor; see the note on Ezra 2:2.

a: Descendants of Arah: 652.
p: About twenty numbers in this list differ from Ezra 2. Hebrew numerals were easy to miscopy.
b: Arah has 652 here and 775 in Ezra 2:5. Other examples: Azgad 2,322 here, 1,222 in Ezra; Adin 655 here, 454 in Ezra; Bethel and Ai 123 here, 223 in Ezra; Senaah 3,930 here, 3,630 in Ezra. Each list keeps its own figures in this translation. Numbers written in words or in numeral signs were easily confused in copying, and many differences differ by one digit. The full table is on the chapter page and on the Ezra 2 page.

a: Descendants of Hariph: 112.
p: Several names differ from Ezra 2: Hariph for Jorah, Binnui for Bani, Hodevah for Hodaviah.
b: The two lists name the same clans in different forms. Hariph here (and in 10:19) stands where Ezra 2:18 has Jorah, with the same number, 112, so it is the same family under another name. Binnui (7:15) and Bani (Ezra 2:10) both come from the root "build." Hodevah (7:43) is a short form of Hodaviah (Ezra 2:40), "praise the LORD." Among the temple servants Nehemiah has Sia for Siaha, Sophereth for Hassophereth and Perida for Peruda (7:47; 7:57). The Plain spells each name as each book's Hebrew has it.

a: People of Gibeon: 95.
p: Ezra 2:20 has 'Gibbar.' Nehemiah's 'Gibeon' fits the town names that follow.
b: Here the list turns from family names to town names. Gibeon, the town north of Jerusalem (3:7; Joshua 9), fits that pattern, and many think Ezra's Gibbar is a slip for it. Others think Gibbar was a real family. Each list keeps its own reading.

a: Men of the other Nebo: 52.
p: Only Nehemiah says 'the other Nebo.' The word 'other' may have slipped in from the next line.
b: Ezra 2:29 has simply "People of Nebo." The next line in both lists is "the other Elam" (7:34; Ezra 2:31), and many think "other" was copied up by mistake. Nebo here is a town in Judah or Benjamin, not the mountain in Moab.

a: The governor
p: The Persian title Tirshatha. In 8:9 and 10:1 it is used of Nehemiah himself; here it probably means an earlier governor.
b: Tirshatha is a Persian title, perhaps "the one to be respected." In the original list it referred to the governor of the first return, Sheshbazzar or Zerubbabel (see the note on Ezra 2:63). But in Nehemiah's book the title is used of Nehemiah (8:9; 10:1), so a reader may hear 7:65 and 7:70 as Nehemiah's rulings and gifts. The Greek translator did: at 7:70 it has the family heads give "to Nehemiah" (see the variant).

a: Taken together, the whole assembly was 42,360,
p: Nehemiah's numbers add to 31,089, Ezra's to 29,818, but both give the total 42,360.
b: Both lists end with the same total, though neither list's numbers add up to it. On the explanations, see the note on Ezra 2:64. The fact that the totals agree while the parts differ suggests that the total was copied more carefully, or came from a separate count.

a: Some of the heads of families gave to the work
p: Nehemiah splits the gifts among the governor, the family heads and the people. Ezra has one lump sum.
b: Ezra 2:69 gives one total: 61,000 drachmas of gold, 5,000 minas of silver and 100 robes. Nehemiah gives three groups: the governor 1,000 drachmas, 50 bowls and 530 robes; the family heads 20,000 drachmas and 2,200 minas; the people 20,000 drachmas, 2,000 minas and 67 robes, so 41,000 drachmas, 4,200 minas and 597 robes in all. Ezra's figures look like rounded totals of a list like this one. The Greek differs in three places: it has the gifts given "to Nehemiah," thirty robes for 530, and 2,200 minas for the people's 2,000, so 4,400 minas in all (see the variants). On drachmas and darics, see the note on Ezra 2:69.

a: The seventh month arrived. The Israelites were in their towns.
p: The same words begin Ezra 3. Here they lead into Ezra's reading of the law; there, into the altar.
b: Ezra 3:1 begins: "The seventh month arrived. The Israelites were in their towns, and the people gathered at Jerusalem, all together as one." Nehemiah 8:1 goes on in almost the same words. In Ezra the gathering builds the altar; in Nehemiah it hears the law. Most English Bibles, like the Hebrew, keep this sentence in 7:73, though it starts the new story; some print it as the start of chapter 8. The shared seam is the strongest sign that one book borrowed the list, with its ending, from the other.
